title: Same question, every model: cross-model scenario battery
about: Battery run on 6 Nov 2026 on the hosted PolicyEngine Macro MCP (adapter 0.2.0). Cells with a stored path were fetched for this file; cells marked 'battery' are the values from the same day's battery (macro#213), stored with their exact call. Committed cells are read from a model repository's own outputs, with no solve. Regenerate the FRB/US cells with models/compare/run_battery.py --refresh frb-us.

boe-1999.label: Bank of England, 1pp rise held one year
boe-1999.text: Output −0.2% to −0.35% after about a year; inflation −0.2 to −0.4pp a year or so after that. 1pp × 4 quarters = 4 pp-quarters, so 0.05–0.09% of GDP per pp-quarter.
boe-1999.source: Bank of England, The transmission mechanism of monetary policy, Quarterly Bulletin 1999 Q2

fed-2014.label: Fed FRB/US, 100bp funds-rate shock (VAR expectations)
fed-2014.text: Output gap trough −0.4pp (FEDS Note 2014); about −0.53pp at quarter 6 (price–wage note 2013, Fig. 3, read off the chart); inflation about −0.08pp.
fed-2014.source: Brayton, Laubach and Reifschneider, FEDS Note, 3 Apr 2014; FRB/US price–wage sector note, Aug 2013, p.16 (quoted in us-frb-model VALIDATION.md, Test 3)

purchases.label: Purchases multiplier, year 1
purchases.text: 0.7–1.0 (Coenen et al. 2012; CBO WP 2015-02). OBR uses 0.6 for current spending on impact, tapering to zero over five years (OBR, Nov 2023).
purchases.source: Coenen et al., AEJ: Macroeconomics 2012; Whalen and Reichling, CBO Working Paper 2015-02; OBR, Dynamic scoring of policy measures in OBR forecasts, Nov 2023

tax.label: Tax multiplier
tax.text: CBO about 0.3 (band 0.15–0.45). OBR household tax 0.3 on impact, decaying.
tax.source: Whalen and Reichling, CBO Working Paper 2015-02; OBR, Dynamic scoring of policy measures in OBR forecasts, Nov 2023

questions.title: What does a 100bp rise in the policy rate do?
questions.experiment: A 1pp rise in the policy rate. The models do not share a rate path, so each row states its own and the size of the path in pp-quarters (annualised rate × quarters).
notes: GDP per pp-quarter divides the peak GDP effect by the rate path's size to the peak. HANK's figure uses the realised real-rate path; the other rows use the nominal policy rate, which is close to the real rate in FRB/US because its inflation barely moves. On HANK's rstar path (10 pp-quarters at ρ = 0.9) the figure would be about 0.04%, so HANK's 0.16 and FRB/US's 0.15 are not like-for-like.
HANK reports inflation as a quarterly rate; this page multiplies it by 4 to give an annual rate.

cells.timing: GDP peaks at q4; no price response
cells.solver: converged: false in all 12 quarters (the iterative solver stalls)
cells.reason: GDP is 3–5× below the BoE 1999 range, through consumption only; inflation and unemployment are exactly zero.

args.shock: 1 s.d. UK monetary-policy shock (+25bp on impact), scaled ×4

cells.rate_path: +25bp on impact, still +0.17pp at h = 12 (a unit root: the rate does not revert); about 1.9 pp-quarters to h = 8 per 25bp

gdp.units: % of GDP, at h = 8, scaled from −0.39% per 25bp

inflation.units: % on the CPI level at h = 20, scaled from −0.63% per 25bp

cells.timing: GDP already −0.14% per s.d. on impact, then flat; no reversion within 5 years
cells.reason: 2–4× the BoE range per pp-quarter and front-loaded, against the BoE's fullest effect after about a year. Bands are wide (186 accepted draws, an effective sample size of 91).

cells.rate_path: +1.00pp on impact, decays under the inertial rule, crosses zero at q8, undershoots
cells.timing: Hump: GDP and inflation peak at q8
cells.verdict_label: Plausible on output; inflation about 40% of published
cells.reason: Output trough sits between the Fed's published −0.4 and −0.53. Inflation is about 40% of the published −0.08pp.

cells.rate_path: Policy-rate shock (rstar) +0.25pp a quarter (= +1pp annualised), AR(1) ρ = 0.9; realised real rate +1.36pp annualised on impact
cells.timing: Both peak on impact; no hump
cells.reason: Inflation is about 40× FRB/US and 3–7× the BoE range, and peaks on impact rather than after about two years, which is consistent with the model's forward-looking Phillips curve. The tool's unit label is easy to misread.

cells.reason: DEFINE-UK has no monetary-policy instrument.

questions.title: Is a 100bp cut the mirror image of a 100bp rise?
questions.experiment: The same experiment with the sign flipped. A linear model gives exactly the opposite answer; the gap is the asymmetry.

cells.symmetry: Peak +0.061 against −0.065 for the rise; at q12 +0.011 against −0.018, so the cut's q12 tail is about 60% the size of the rise's. A tail of 0.01–0.02% persists after the shock ends.
cells.reason: Not symmetric: the persistent tail is solver residue about the size of a 25bp signal.
A linear VAR: the cut is the exact negative of the rise. Its size is off; see the +100bp question.
Close to symmetric; FRB/US is nonlinear, so a small gap is expected.

cells.symmetry: Exact mirror: responses are first-order around the steady state.
cells.reason: Linear by construction, so this tests nothing beyond the +100bp run.
DEFINE-UK has no monetary-policy instrument.

questions.title: Is a 25bp rise a quarter of a 100bp rise?
questions.experiment: A 25bp rise, compared with the 100bp result divided by four. A linear model gives the same GDP effect per 100bp at both sizes.

cells.linearity: Peak GDP per 100bp: 0.100 at 25bp, 0.065 at 100bp, 0.060 at 200bp. Not proportional: 1.53× per bp at 25bp.
cells.solver: converged: false in all 12 quarters; the stall residue is the size of the 25bp signal
cells.reason: Small shocks are not proportional because the solve does not converge.
A linear VAR. Its size is off; see the +100bp question.
Close to proportional.

cells.linearity: Exact: responses scale with the shock size.
cells.reason: Linear by construction, so this tests nothing beyond the +100bp run.
DEFINE-UK has no monetary-policy instrument.

questions.title: What does government spending of 1% of GDP do to output?
questions.experiment: Higher government purchases worth about 1% of GDP. The multiplier is the GDP change divided by the spending change, both in % of GDP. Financing and the monetary rule differ by model and drive most of the spread.
notes: FRB/US's hosted tool cannot run a sustained +1%-of-GDP experiment: the stored run is a one-quarter impulse of about 0.046% of GDP, and the year-1 figure comes from a committed sustained run (macro #212).

cells.experiment: CGG +£7,000m a quarter (about 1.0% of GDP) for 4 quarters

gdp.units: % of GDP, peak (+1.011% to +1.025% over q1–q4, about 0 from q5)

cells.solver: converged: false in all 12 quarters; the tool's own caveat calls the result an upper bound
cells.reason: An accounting identity, not a multiplier. The OBR's own figure is 0.6, tapering.
The BoE SVAR identifies no fiscal shock.

cells.experiment: Federal purchases +1% (about 0.046% of GDP), one quarter

gdp.units: % of GDP, peak, per 0.046% of GDP spent

cells.multiplier: about 0.81 on impact; 0.725 in year 1 for a committed sustained run (inertial rule)
cells.reason: Inside the 0.7–1.0 band.

cells.experiment: G +1% of GDP on impact, AR(1) ρ = 0.8, financed by the labour tax
cells.multiplier: 0.175 (ρ = 0.8); 0.075 at ρ = 0.9. Output turns negative from q3 while spending is still 51–73% of impact
cells.reason: A balanced-budget multiplier can be below 1, but investment falls 2.6% and consumption 0.5–0.7% on impact, the sign flips while spending is still high, and the answer halves between ρ = 0.8 and 0.9. The 0.7–1.0 range above is the published purchases multiplier (Coenen et al.; CBO); this run is financed by the labour tax, so it is not directly comparable, and no balanced-budget benchmark is sourced.

path.inflation_units: pp, quarterly rate (pi); × 4 for an annual rate

cells.multiplier: 1.78, 2.30 or 1.94 depending on how the impulse is defined
cells.reason: The impulse definition is not settled, and an annual, investment-led scenario is not comparable to a 4-quarter purchases shock. No published benchmark.

questions.title: What does a 1pp rise in the personal tax rate do?
questions.experiment: A rise in the effective personal income-tax rate of about 1pp.
notes: FRB/US with periods = 4 stacks the tax add-factor to +2.37pp rather than +1pp, and the tool's label does not warn (macro #212). The stored run uses periods = 1.

cells.multiplier: 0.15 in year 1, rising to 0.34 by q12
cells.reason: Right order of magnitude, but it rises where the OBR's 0.3 decays.
The BoE SVAR identifies no tax shock.

cells.experiment: +1pp on the effective personal rate on impact, decaying to +0.05pp by q8
cells.multiplier: 0.22 in year 1, 0.32 in year 2 (committed tax-cut run)
cells.reason: Inside the CBO band of 0.15–0.45.
The labour tax is endogenous in US HANK, so there is no tax-rate instrument.
No income-tax instrument in the committed scenarios.

questions.title: What does a rise in oil and energy prices do?
questions.experiment: A rise in the oil price of about $10 a barrel. No sourced magnitude benchmark exists for any model, so only the sign and the transmission are judged.
notes: FRB/US's tool labels the oil lever's units 'model units'; they are dollars a barrel, so +10 is +15.4% on the oil price (macro #212).

cells.reason: The price block does not respond to the oil price.

cells.result: Bank Rate does not significantly respond: the 68% set straddles zero at h = 0–8, as the paper's text says.
cells.reason: Magnitudes are not benchmarked.

inflation.units: % on the CPI level, on impact

cells.result: The funds rate eases by 0.017pp, because the rule targets core inflation; everything reverts within a quarter of the shock ending, with no second-round effects.
cells.reason: No sourced benchmark for the size. Core PCE falls 0.005pp after the oil rise; the cause is not yet diagnosed.

cells.reason: US HANK has no energy-price instrument.
